# Diabetes Data Description

Scenario: You are a health analytics consultant that has been asked to perform an exploratory data analysis regarding diabetes. You are given a dataset containing information for 100 randomly sampled patients from all patients at a specific hospital. The dataset includes the following:

-   **Gender**: Their gender (Male or Female)
-   **Diabetes_Type**: Their type of diabetes
-   **Age**: Their age (in *whole* years, no decimals)
-   **Smoking_Status**: Their smoking status (current, former, or never)
-   **Number_of_Visits**: The number of times they've visited the hospital
-   **Exercise_Frequency**: How often they exercise
-   **Fasting_Blood_Sugar**: Their blood sugar level while fasting (mg/dL)
-   **HbA1c**: Glucose attached to hemoglobin in red blood cells (mmol/mol)

```{r, echo = TRUE}
suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(library(ggplot2)))
suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(library(dplyr)))

diabetes_data <- read.csv("../data/diabetes_data.csv") # Fill in the path to the dataset
attach(diabetes_data)
```

Complete the questions below by filling in the blanks with the appropriate answers or by providing the necessary R code.

## Question 1 (4 points)

Below is a histogram of Fasting_Blood_Sugar.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
ggplot(diabetes_data, aes(x = Fasting_Blood_Sugar)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Fasting Blood Sugar",
       x = "Fasting Blood Sugar (mg/dL)",
       y = "Frequency")
```

Using this histogram, what would you say is the skewness of the distribution? [This distribution is mostly symmetric. You could also possibly say there is a *very slight* left-skew. Most people would say it is symmetric, but both of these answers could be considered correct.]{style="color: red;"}

Based on the skew, would you expect the mean to be less than, greater than, or approximately equal to the median? [If you say that the distribution looks symmetric, then you would expect the mean and median to be very close to one another. If you believe there is a very slight left skew, then you would say that the mean is less than the median.]{style="color: red;"}

Compute and display the mean and median for Fasting_Blood_Sugar below.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
mean(Fasting_Blood_Sugar)

median(Fasting_Blood_Sugar)
```

[The two are very close to one another because of the symmetry of the distribution. The mean is slightly less than the median indicating that there is a *slight* left skew.]{style="color: red;"}

## Question 2 (1 point)

Below is a histogram of Number_of_Visits.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
ggplot(diabetes_data, aes(x = Number_of_Visits)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Number of Visits",
       x = "Number of Visits",
       y = "Frequency")
```

Based on the histogram, would you say the distribution is unimodal, bimodal, or multimodal? [This distribution is multimodal. There appear to be three major peaks.]{style="color: red;"}

## Question 4 (2 points)

Produce a visualization for the following variables:

### HbA1c

[The dataset has 100 observations, which is somewhere between a small and medium sized dataset. Any of the following charts would work alright.]{style="color: red;"}

```{r, echo = TRUE}
diabetes_data %>% ggplot(aes(x = HbA1c)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.3, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of HbA1c") +
  ylab("Frequency")
```

```{r, echo = TRUE}
diabetes_data %>% ggplot(aes(x = HbA1c)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of HbA1c") +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

```{r, echo = TRUE}
diabetes_data %>% ggplot(aes(x = HbA1c)) + 
  geom_dotplot() +
  labs(title = "Dot Chart of HbA1c") +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
      axis.text.y = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

```{r, echo = TRUE}
stem(HbA1c, scale = 2)
```

### Exercise_Frequency

[Either a bar chart of a pie chart could be used, although it is recommended that one use a bar chart.]{style="color: red;"}

```{r, echo = TRUE}
diabetes_data %>% ggplot(aes(x = Exercise_Frequency)) + 
  geom_bar() +
  xlab("Exercise Frequency") +
  labs(title = "Bar Chart of Exercise Frequency") +
  ylab("Frequency")
```

```{r, echo = TRUE}
diabetes_data %>% ggplot(aes(x = factor(1), fill = factor(Exercise_Frequency))) + 
  geom_bar(width = 1) + coord_polar(theta = "y") + 
  labs(title = "Pie Chart of Exercise Frequency") +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
      axis.text.y = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
      axis.title.x = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) +
  scale_fill_discrete(name = "Exercise Frequency")
```
